ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint/trigger: Mild breathing difficulty and concern for lip swelling moments after a presumed wasp/bee sting to right arm.  
• Symptom timeline: Sting occurred “a few minutes ago.” Immediate local redness; patient felt dyspnoea, lip tingling, “weird” tongue sensation. No progression at time of call.  
• ENT symptoms:
  – Throat swelling/closure sensation: none reported.  
  – Voice change/hoarseness: none.  
  – Dysphagia/odynophagia/drooling: none.  
  – Nasal/ocular symptoms: none.  
  – Stridor/noisy breathing: none heard or reported.  
  – Dyspnea: subjective, mild; able to speak full sentences.  
  – Swelling distribution: patient perceives slight right-sided lip swelling; not visible to clinician. Tongue feels “weird,” no visible edema. No facial or uvular swelling.  
  – Ear/neck symptoms: none.  
• Past episodes/treatment: No prior anaphylaxis; never prescribed epinephrine auto-injector.  
• Allergies: Penicillin (reaction details not documented).  
• Current medications: None. Rescue meds: none. Antihistamine not yet taken.  
• Medical history: Eczema; occasional anxiety/panic episodes (never medicated).  
• Social: 27-year-old male computer scientist; lives alone with a cat.

Objective:
• Visible swelling: None of lips, tongue, or face. Sting site with mild erythema and puncture mark, no significant swelling or heat.  
• Airway/breathing: Normal work of breathing; clear speech; no stridor.  
• Mental status: Alert, oriented; mildly anxious.  
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• Examined via video; patient alone.

Assessment:
Working impression: Localized allergic reaction to insect sting with mild subjective dyspnoea; no current evidence of systemic anaphylaxis or airway compromise.

Evidence summary: Immediate arm erythema after sting, subjective lip/tongue symptoms, normal video airway exam, stable speech, no visible edema or respiratory distress.

DDx (aligned with transcript):
1. Localized allergic reaction to insect venom – most likely; supported by isolated cutaneous findings without systemic signs.  
2. Early IgE-mediated anaphylaxis – possible; timing within minutes and patient-reported dyspnoea warrant caution despite normal exam.  
3. Anxiety/panic response – contributory; history of anxiety and mismatch between symptoms and objective findings.

Plan:
• Pharmacologic: Start oral antihistamine (e.g., Chlorphenamine 4 mg PO; may repeat up to 6×/day OR once-daily non-sedating alternative).  
• Monitoring/precautions:  
  – Remain vigilant for red-flag symptoms: lip/tongue/facial swelling, voice change, throat tightness, stridor, increasing dyspnoea, generalized urticaria, dizziness/syncope.  
  – If any red-flag develops, proceed immediately to Emergency Department or call emergency services (999).  
• Education: Provided verbal and electronic information on signs of anaphylaxis and when to seek urgent care. Reassured that current presentation appears localized.  
• Follow-up: Contact GP/ENT urgently if deterioration; routine follow-up not required unless recurrent reactions occur. No immediate need for formal allergy testing or epinephrine auto-injector at this time; reassess if future systemic reaction occurs.  
• Additional: Advised to observe sting site; if erythema spreads, becomes hot, or systemic infection signs arise, seek medical review for possible antibiotics.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Expected but missing: vital signs; detailed penicillin reaction history; confirmation of tetanus status; documentation of antihistamine brand/dose supplied; formal airway measurements; availability of epinephrine auto-injector plan.  
● Transcript/DDx conflicts: none significant noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear audio; minor conversational fillers but clinically adequate.
